**The Quiet Rebellion of Being Curious**

I’ve been thinking about how most of us are secretly running away from the same thing: the feeling that we’re supposed to have already figured life out.

We scroll, we optimize, we perform competence on LinkedIn and Instagram, we chase the next milestone like it’s a high-score that will finally quiet the background hum. But the hum never leaves. It’s not anxiety, exactly. It’s *wonder* that’s been muzzled. The same wonder that made us, at age six, ask why the sky is blue and what happens when you die and whether dogs dream in color. That version of us didn’t need productivity hacks. It was already whole.

The older we get, the more we treat curiosity like a hobby instead of the main operating system. We schedule it between meetings. We outsource it to podcasts we half-listen to while doing the dishes. We consume other people’s curiosity instead of living our own.

But every now and then the mask slips.

You catch a documentary about deep-sea creatures at 2 a.m. and suddenly you’re crying because the universe made something that glows in the dark and has no eyes and somehow that feels profoundly hopeful. Or you’re driving home from a perfectly fine day and a song hits you like a truck and for thirty seconds you remember that existence is ridiculous and miraculous at the same time. These moments aren’t interruptions. They’re the real signal. Everything else is noise we agreed to call normal.

I think the highest form of rebellion available to us right now isn’t political or even artistic. It’s choosing to stay stupid on purpose, in the best way. To keep asking questions that don’t have immediate applications. To waste time staring at clouds or talking to strangers or learning something you’ll never monetize. To protect the part of you that still gets stupidly excited about things.

The world is optimized to the point of sterility. But life—real life—has always been a little bit embarrassing. It involves enthusiasm and bewilderment and changing your mind in public. It requires you to say, without irony, “I don’t know… but I want to.”

So this is my completely unasked-for manifesto:

Stay porous.  
Stay amateur.  
Stay in love with the sheer ridiculous fact that anything exists at all.

The universe spent 13.8 billion years setting up the conditions for you to be here, right now, feeling whatever the hell you’re feeling. The least we can do is notice.

And maybe, just maybe, stay curious enough to be slightly inconvenient to the parts of ourselves and our culture that want us quiet, predictable, and finally “done.”

The hum is still there, isn’t it?

Good.  
Follow it.
